paper_title: Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.

Top-left: Traditional pipelines reduce diverse sources to isolated QAs. Bottom-left: TOME-Math preserves textbook structure through structured QA construction and curriculumbased SFT. Right: TOME-Math comprises 380,292 QAs from 2,118 textbooks spanning 29 subjects. *Equal contribution, Corresponding authors. Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks 1. Introduction Mathematical reasoning in large language models has advanced rapidly, driven in part by improvements in training data and in part by advances in reasoning-time computation [1, 2, 4, 10, 13, 15, 21, 2729, 37, 38, 42]. On the data side, recent efforts have expanded mathematical supervision to millions of QA pairs (i.e., QuestionAnswer pairs) and in doing so have revealed that properties such as question diversity, solution format, and teacher-model quality significantly shape downstream performance [18, 31, 39, 40]. These findings suggest broader principle: The value of mathematical supervision is not determined by the number of training examples alone, but also by how those examples are constructed and organized. Despite this, the dominant paradigm for mathematical supervision remains the isolated problemsolution pair. Whether the original knowledge comes from competition archives, grade-school word problems, web exercises, or synthetic augmentation, the resulting training data typically takes the uniform shape of problem solution [7, 14, 39]. This representation is convenient to scale, but it does not explicitly leverage the organizational structure that many source materials already possess. Mathematical textbooks are notable case in point. textbook is not merely collection of solved problems, but carefully structured body of knowledge. Definitions introduce core concepts, lemmas and theorems develop them, proofs establish their validity, and exercises reinforce understanding. These elements are organized within chapter hierarchy that reflects prerequisite relations, conceptual dependencies, and pedagogical progression. Prior work has explored textbooks as source of mathematical pretraining data, problemsolution pairs, and proof supervision [3, 16, 19, 30, 33, 35, 41]. However, textbooks are often treated primarily as sources of mathematical content, leaving their native structure underexplored. In particular, it remains unclear how to scale natural-language proof supervision while preserving chapter order, proposition dependencies, source locations, and exercises in unified framework. To address this gap, we introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), large-scale proof-supervision resource constructed from 2,118 mathematics textbooks. Central to TOME-Math is the notion of structured mathematical supervision, which preserves structure at three levels. First, hierarchical structure retains the native organization of textbooks, including chapters, propositions, and their ordering. Second, dependency structure connects theorem-level proof questions with the intermediate proof obligations derived from gaps in their proofs. Third, curriculum structure organizes supervision according to textbook order and proof granularity, enabling controlled training over related examples rather than independent QA pairs. Following these principles, TOME-Math contains 380,292 proof-oriented QA pairs spanning 29 mathematical subjects. Figure 1 provides an overview of the construction and organization of the resulting corpus. We further validate the effectiveness of TOME-Math through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 30B base model [38]. Its retained structure enables controlled studies of how the organization of supervision affects mathematical reasoning. Rather than treating scale as the only variable, TOME-Math allows us to examine the roles of retrieval structure, curriculum order, and source coverage under controlled settings. Empirically, TOME-Math SFT improves the six-benchmark average from 29.17% to 45.83%, while further experiments show consistent benefits from structure-guided retrieval, textbook-aligned curricula, and broader source coverage. Our contributions are: We introduce TOME-Math, large-scale proof-supervision resource constructed from 2,118 mathematics textbooks. Through structure-preserving pipeline, it produces 380,292 Concept and Gap QA records while retaining chapter progression, propositionproof links, dependency references, source provenance, and separate inventory of textbook-authored exercises. We demonstrate the overall effectiveness of TOME-Math through full-corpus fine-tuning. On book-heldout textbook exercises and established public benchmarks, TOME-Math achieves the best performance on five of six evaluations, improving the unweighted six-benchmark mean from 29.17% to 45.83% over the base model and outperforming all three public instruction-data baselines in aggregate. We systematically investigate how textbook structure contributes to mathematical reasoning at inference and training time. Structure-guided retrieval improves proof-generation pass@1 from 13.25% to 17.38% under matched context budget; across six subjects and three data scales, forward textbook curricula consistently outperform shuffled and reverse schedules; and broader source coverage yields further gains under fixed training-token budget. 2 Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks Table 1: Mathematical resources by scale, supervision, and structure. Section/exercise IDs Lean statements Statement tags Proof judgments NL + local proofs Chapter order, refs, provenance 2. Related Work Mathematical instruction data. GSM8K and MATH provide human-authored problems and solutions for grade-school and competition mathematics [7, 14]. MetaMathQA and OpenMathInstruct-2 scale these seeds through synthetic augmentation [31, 39], while NuminaMath-CoT aggregates diverse sources with chain-ofthought solutions [20]. Their primary supervision unit is problemsolution pair, accompanied by source, seed-question, or difficulty metadata. Table 1 contrasts this organization with the textbook hierarchy and proposition links retained by TOME-Math. Textbook and knowledge-informed resources. OpenWebMath and MathPile provide mathematical pretraining text, with MathPile incorporating textbooks alongside papers and web sources [25, 33]. CollegeMath extracts textbook exercises and short answers, while MathScale synthesizes QA using graph of topics and knowledge points [30]. TheoremQA evaluates theorem application across STEM subjects [6]. These efforts motivate retaining both textbook organization and links to mathematical statements when constructing proof supervision. Proof resources and evaluation. NaturalProofs preserves statements, proofs, and reference graph [35, 36], while NaturalProofs-Gen and NaturalProver study reference-grounded proof generation . Proof Net and LeanGAP connect textbook mathematics to formalization [3, 19], while FormaRLs uproof provides 5,273 proof problems from 14 textbooks for autoformalization evaluation [16]. Proof2Hybrids AlgGeoTest studies proofderived judgments, and the Open Proof Corpus studies automated assessment of human-evaluated model proofs [8, 26]. Building on these directions, TOME-Math combines coverage of 2,118 textbooks with selfcontained local proof obligations, chapter order, and proposition references, supporting controlled studies of source coverage, proof-target format, and training order. 3. TOME-Math 3.1. Data Construction Pipeline overview. We construct TOME-Math through structure-preserving pipeline that converts raw textbook PDFs into two complementary forms of proof supervision: Proof QA derived from explicit proposition proof units and Gap QA derived from missing proof obligations in Proof QAs. The source collection is selected against university course syllabi and reviewed by domain experts, yielding 2,118 input PDFs after canonicalization and deduplication (as shown in Section 3.2). The pipeline generated the full TOME-Math dataset of 380,292 QA pairs, comprising 174,431 Gap QA pairs and 205,861 Proof QA pairs. 3 Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks Figure 2: Overview of TOME-Math construction, from structured textbook parsing and chapter recovery to Proof QA extraction, Gap QA generation, and quality-controlled corpus assembly (Section 3.1). Document parsing and structured chapter extraction. DeepSeek-OCR [34] converts each PDF into multimodal Markdown together with page images. page-wise gpt-oss-120b [23] pass separates the table of contents and main body from covers, prefaces, and other front matter, then reconstructs hierarchical table of contents. Conditioned on this hierarchy, state machine reads the body in order, judges whether each page belongs to the current chapter, the next chapter, or contains an internal boundary, and retries ambiguous assignments before updating the chapter state. This produces an ordered set of chapter-level documents while preserving the textbook hierarchy. second page-wise pass separates expository core concepts from textbook exercises within each chapter. The exercises are retained as an independent reservoir, but are excluded from the Proof QA generation path. Proof QA Extraction and Gap QA construction. For each core concept chapter, we use gemini-3.1flash-lite-preview [12] to extract theoremproof, lemmaproof, and definitionproof units and retrieve the earlier propositions needed to interpret each proof. These source-grounded units form the Proof QA stream. We then use gemini-3-flash-preview with thinking enabled [11] to inspect each proof for gaps (i.e., implicit or missing reasoning steps). When substantive gap is detected, gemini-3.1-flashlite-preview [12] rewrites the missing obligation as self-contained proposition and completes its proof, producing the Gap QA stream. This structured construction preserves explicit textbook proofs while adding targeted supervision for intermediate reasoning that the source leaves unstated. Validation and quality control. Quality control is applied at both the structural and semantic levels. The structural checks validate the table-of-contents hierarchy, ambiguous page boundaries, question continuity across pages, questionanswer alignment, and standalone completeness. For proposition extraction, sourceconditioned gpt-oss-120b judge audits candidates along five axes: completeness, accuracy, LATEX formatting, self-containment, and atomicity. Accuracy is treated as critical: invented proof steps, altered mathematical relations, or other content not supported by the source are failure cases rather than stylistic defects. Full module logic, intermediate artifacts, model-allocation details, and the judging rubric are given in Appendix A. 3.2. Characterization TOME-Math comprises 380,292 QA records from 2,118 canonical textbooks across 29 subject categories, summarized in Figure 3. Appendix provides the detailed corpus characterization, including subject and language coverage, task composition, structural complexity, confidence dynamics, quality, and provenance. 4 Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks (a) Dataset construction and filtering. (b) Model-quality comparison. Figure 3: TOME-Math data composition and quality characterization. (L): dataset scale from source textbooks through filtering to the final corpus. (R): model configurations compared across the quality-control criteria. Generation Composition. The corpus combines Proof QA stream of 205,861 records and Gap QA stream of 174,431 records, drawing on disjoint model assignments (Appendix B). gemini-3-flash-preview -thinking [11] produces 88.9% of Proof QA records, gpt-5-mini [22] produces 53.7% of Gap QA records, and the Gap QA stream retains 174,431 of 918,235 generated candidates, yield of 19.00%. Model-quality trade-off. We evaluate model-quality trade-off along six dimensions, and combine gemini-3 -flash-preview-thinking (Flash Thinking) for primary extraction and auditing with gemini-3.1 -flash-lite-preview (Flash Lite) for reference-semantic parsing, balancing quality and cost. See more details in Appendix A.6 Provenance and Evaluation Units. Each record carries book, chapter, and source location metadata, with proposition identifiers and resolved references for Proof QA records. We define two evaluation scopes at the book level, held out exercises for item level generalization and held out books for source level generalization, both respecting duplicate groups identified by global content hash. 4. Evaluating TOME-Math 4.1. Experimental Setup Base Model. We use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base [38] as the backbone for all experiments. All SFT variants start from the same checkpoint, and the unmodified checkpoint serves as the base-model baseline. Evaluation. To obtain sensitive view of how structured textbook supervision affects learning, we focus on the six core subjects with the largest usable textbook collections in our corpus: abstract algebra, differential geometry, discrete mathematics, mathematical analysis, probability, and topology. We construct TOMELONGFORM from their textbook-authored exercises: 300 proof-heavy problems from held-out books, balanced across subjects and the earlier and later halves of each book. To enforce book-level separation, we reserve 64 source books for evaluation and exclude all 15,661 QA records associated with those books from the complete 380,292-record TOME-Math corpus. This leaves 364,631 examples in the actual training split. The evaluation problems are selected separately from the native-exercise reservoir of the held-out books. We sample 16 solutions per problem and score them with reference-guided step verifier; each solution is reviewed eight times by gpt-5.6-luna [24] and is accepted only if no review identifies substantive error. For complementary coverage beyond long-form proofs, TOME-OBJECTIVE contains 145 multidisciplinary objective problems scored by final-answer equivalence. We additionally evaluate on MiniF2F [43], Proof Net [3], MATH-500 [14], and AIME2026 [9]. Full construction and scoring details are given in Appendix D. 5 Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks Table 2: Full-corpus comparison of models independently fine-tuned on each listed SFT corpus. Evaluation covers TOME-LONGFORM (TOME-LF.), TOME-OBJECTIVE(TOME-OBJ.), MiniF2F, Proof Net, MATH-500, and AIME 2026. Scores are reported as percentages; Avg. is the unweighted mean of the six reported scores. Best and second-best results in each column are shown in bold and underlined, respectively. Full-Corpus Comparison We first present the overall effectiveness of the final TOME-Math dataset, before isolating its structural components in Section 5. Table 2 compares the resulting 364,631-example TOME-Math training split with three public mathematics SFT corpora at their available scales. All fine-tuned models start from Qwen3-30B-A3BBase and use the same fine-tuning setup, differing only in their supervision corpus; each model is trained for one full epoch over its respective corpus, and the unmodified checkpoint is included as reference. Complete training configurations are provided in Appendix E.2. Aggregate performance. TOME-Math achieves the best result on five of the six benchmarks and ranks second on AIME 2026. Its largest margins over the strongest public baseline appear on the proof-oriented TOMELONGFORM and Proof Net evaluations, while its advantages on TOME-OBJECTIVE, MiniF2F, and MATH-500 show that the benefit extends beyond its own evaluation distribution and is not confined to long-form proof generation. Averaged uniformly across the six reported scores, TOME-Math improves the base-model mean from 29.17% to 45.83%, gain of 16.66 percentage points (16.7 when rounded to one decimal). Effect of supervision corpus. The ranking is not explained by corpus size alone. OpenMath1 contains 1.82M examples, approximately 4.8 the size of TOME-Mathyet TOME-Math outperforms it on all six benchmarks. It also exceeds the similarly sized MetaMath corpus throughout and improves consistently over the pretrained backbone. These results demonstrate the overall utility of TOME-Math and suggest that the source and form of supervision matter in addition to raw example count. Because the corpora differ in several respects, the comparison does not by itself isolate textbook structure as the causal factor; we examine that structure through controlled retrieval and training studies in Section 5. 5. Leveraging Textbook Structure Beyond providing large source of proof supervision, TOME-Math exposes structural signalschapter progression, proposition dependencies, and source provenancethat can be used explicitly at inference time and during training. This section investigates when these signals improve mathematical reasoning. We first evaluate structure-guided retrieval without updating model parameters (Section 5.1). We then study whether textbook order provides an effective curriculum under controlled budgets (Section 5.2), and examine source breadth together with transfer to held-out books from other mathematical fields (Section 5.3). Finally, we examine how these structural choices contribute to the full-corpus TOME-Math training recipe (Section 5.4). 5.1. Training-Free Structure-Guided Retrieval Question and design. Can textbook structure identify useful evidence for mathematical problem solving? We test five paired context policies on all 300 TOME-LONGFORM problems using frozen Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base model: (i) CLOSED uses no external context; (ii) RANDOM SAME-BOOK samples uniformly from the exercises source book; (iii) LOCAL CHAPTER draws only from the exercise chapter and its immediate predecessors; (iv) TOME (PROPS ONLY) retrieves propositionproof records using chapter position and recovered dependencies; and (v) TOME (PROPS + GAP) extends the same policy to include Gap QA. Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks Table 3: Training-free structure-guided retrieval on TOME-LONGFORM. Scores are pass@1 (%) on the same 300 problems. Avg. is the mean over six equally sized subjects; the remaining columns report individual subjects. Best results are bolded. See Section 5.1 for details.

All context-augmented conditions receive the same context-token budget. They also share the same backbone, prompt, decoding configuration, and reference-guided verifier; the target exercise and material overlapping its reference answer are removed from every retrieval pool. The resulting comparison asks how effectively each policy selects fixed amount of same-source evidence, rather than whether additional test-time tokens alone help. Appendix gives the complete retrieval, leakage-control, generation, and scoring protocol. Results. The results show clear progression as increasingly structured evidence is introduced. Starting from 13.25% pass@1 in the CLOSED setting, RANDOM SAME-BOOK and LOCAL CHAPTER reach 14.00% and 14.71%, respectively. Retrieving propositionproof records with textbook structure further improves performance to 15.54%, while augmenting this inventory with Gap QA yields the best overall score of 17.38%, 4.13-point gain over closed-book generation. In particular, Gap QA contributes an additional 1.84 points over proposition-only retrieval, showing that explicit local proof obligations provide complementary evidence beyond textbook propositions. Among the four context-augmented conditions, the shared token budget shows that their performance differences arise from evidence selection rather than context quantity. The advantage of the complete TOME (PROPS + GAP) policy is consistent across all six subjects, with improvements of 1.756.00 points over CLOSED. Mathematical analysis and topology show the largest gains (+6.00 points each), while every other subject also improves. By contrast, random same-book or local-chapter context occasionally leaves performance unchanged or lowers it, indicating that access to nearby textbook material alone is not sufficient. Together, these results establish the retained textbook structure as an effective inference-time evidence index and show that proposition context and explicit proof obligations work best in combination. 5.2. Curriculum Learning Across Subjects and Data Scales The retrieval study shows that textbook structure can guide the selection of useful evidence at inference time. We next ask whether the same organization can also improve learning when it is used to order supervision, and whether any benefit persists across subjects and data scales. Setup and comparisons. We evaluate textbook-aligned curricula across six subjects and three per-subject target-token budgets: 0.75M, 1.8M, and 2.4M. Within each subjectscale cell, four schedules reorder the same frozen QA set: SHUFFLE, FORWARDGAP, REVERSEGAP, and FORWARDMIX. Here, Gap QA makes locally omitted proof obligation explicit. FORWARDGAP versus REVERSEGAP isolates chapter direction under fixed Gap-first policy, while FORWARDGAP versus FORWARDMIX isolates Gap-first ordering under fixed forward progression; comparison with SHUFFLE measures their combined effect. All schedules share the same examples, token budget, initialization, and optimization settings, and are evaluated on the same held-outbook exercises. Appendix details the normalized chapter stages, schedule construction, nested data scales, and order-preserving training controls. Overall effect of scale and curriculum. Figure 4 shows that every fine-tuned condition outperforms the shared base checkpoint in all six subjects, even at 0.75M tokens, and that every schedule improves with scale in each subject. Across the 0.75M, 1.8M, and 2.4M budgets, macro-average pass@16 rises from 41.04% to 42.52% and 43.21% for SHUFFLE, and from 45.38% to 48.98% and 50.93% for FORWARDGAP. FORWARDGAP is strongest in all 18 subjectscale cells, and its macro-average margin over SHUFFLE widens from 4.34 points at 0.75M tokens to 6.46 at 1.8M and 7.72 at 2.4M. Controlled comparisons attribute most of this benefit to chapter direction: relative to REVERSEGAP, the forward schedule gains 5.65, 7.41, and 8.50 points across the three scales. Thus, forward progression is the primary contributor, with Gap-first ordering providing complementary gain. The same ordering across all 18 subjectscale cells shows that these benefits persist across mathematical domains and supervision budgets. 5.3. Figure 5(a) compares the 8-book NARROWDENSE condition with BROADSPARSE, which distributes the same 0.75M-token FORWARDGAP budget across 16 books while holding all other settings fixed. BROADSPARSE improves pass@16 in every subject by 1.64.8 points (3.3 on average), with the largest gains in topology (+4.8), differential geometry (+4.4), and discrete mathematics (+3.6). Thus, source breadth is distinct scaling axis: the same supervision budget is more effective when spread across twice as many books. Together with the monotonic gains in Section 5.2, this result shows that textbook supervision benefits from both greater volume and broader coverage. Table 12 details the source pools and QA counts. Cross-subject generalization. Figure 5(b) evaluates each subject-specific 0.75M-token checkpoint on 50 exercises from every other field, normalized by the target specialists in-domain score, Tst = Pst/Ptt. The macro-average transfer coefficient is 0.92. Topology (0.98) and differential geometry (0.97) have the strongest source-side means, and eight of the 30 ordered pairs exceed 1.0; both fields reach 1.29 on probability targets. This strong off-diagonal performance shows that subject-specific supervision develops reusable proof and reasoning patterns rather than benefits confined to its training field. It also supports multidisciplinary training at full scale. Full results are in Appendix H. Taken together, the matched-budget breadth gains and cross-subject transfer connect the controlled studies to the full TOME-Math corpus. Scaling to more books adds source coverage without increasing the token budget, while scaling across subjects supplies supervision that generalizes beyond its domain. These complementary effects explain the effectiveness of the broad, multidisciplinary corpus beyond example count alone. 5.4. Full-Corpus Ablation of the TOME-Math Training Recipe Finally, we ablate curriculum order, Gap-first scheduling, and Gap QA from the full FORWARDGAP recipe and report pass@1 (%) for all variants. All variants use the book-held-out training split described in Section 4. Component contributions. Table 4 shows that every ablation lowers pass@1 across all six benchmarks. On the two TOME benchmarks, replacing Gap-first with within-stage mixing costs 3.74 and 2.59 points, while global shuffling costs another 0.25 and 0.95 points. Thus, Gap-first is the primary ordering signal, complemented by forward chapter progression. Removing Gap QA causes the largest drops on the four proof benchmarks (5.056.77 points), confirming the value of explicit local proof obligations. The complete recipe also leads on MATH-500 and AIME-26, extending the gains beyond proof-focused evaluations. Structural synergy. The ablations reveal mutually reinforcing relationship between TOME-Maths corpus construction and training strategy. Gap QA introduces explicit proof obligations, Gap-first scheduling prioritizes them within each stage, and forward progression exploits the preserved textbook order. The consistent gains across textbook-derived proof tasks, public proof benchmarks, and competition problems establish TOME-Maths advantage as structured supervision beyond scale alone. 6. Conclusion We introduced TOME-Math, corpus of 380K proof records from 2,118 textbooks that preserves curricular and dependency structure. It improves performance across textbook-derived and public benchmarks, while controlled studies demonstrate the benefits of structure-guided retrieval, curriculum ordering, and broader source coverage. We hope TOME-Math inspires mathematical reasoning systems that learn not only from more data, but from better-organized knowledge. 9 Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks

TOME-Math Construction Details This appendix expands the construction stages summarized in Section 3.1. We distinguish the artifacts produced by the book-structure modules (M1M3), exercise and answer processing (M4M6), and the downstream proposition-extraction track. A.1. Intermediate representation DeepSeek-OCR produces one multimodal-Markdown representation of the complete book together with the extracted images. The automated modules materialize the following intermediate artifacts: Artifact toc.json main_text.md images/ Contents Multilevel table of contents represented by title and heading depth. Textbook body after removing front matter. Merged image directory with normalized references from the Markdown files. One Markdown file for every recovered chapter. Chapter text after exercise segments are removed. Chapter-indexed exercise text and formatted per-chapter JSONL files. content/ content_pure/ exercise/ exercise_index.jsonl Multilevel heading path for every exercise section. answer.md detached answer chapter when one is present. A.2. M1M2: Table-of-contents and chapter recovery M1: front matter and table of contents. Starting from the first parsed page, the structure model decides whether page contains table-of-contents entries and whether the textbook body has begun. For contents pages it extracts pairs of the form {title, level}. Pages that are neither contents nor body are treated as cover or front matter and are discarded. Once the body is detected, verification pass corrects invalid heading depths and removes entries that belong to prefaces or notation lists. If the model detects body text before extracting any valid contents entries, the whole module is retried, up to five attempts. M1 emits toc.json, main_text.md, and the merged images/ directory. M2: hierarchy-conditioned segmentation. The recovered contents are traversed as tree. Internal entries direct the traversal to their children, while leaf entries trigger search for the corresponding body span. For each page and the current/next chapter titles, the model returns one of three states: ALL-CURRENT (the page belongs to the current chapter), ALL-NEXT (it belongs to the next chapter), or BOUNDARY (the transition occurs within the page). Boundary pages are checked second time; failed check is fed back to the assignment step. successful transition advances the state machine and writes the completed chapter to content/. A.3. M3M6: Exercise extraction and answer alignment M3: exercise separation. The structure model first tests whether the table of contents contains dedicated exercise chapters. When it does, those chapters are detached directly. When it does not, each content chapter is scanned for trailing block of exercises, which is removed from the exposition. The same module constructs the multilevel exercise-title index and detects separate answer chapter, if present. Its outputs are content_pure/, exercise/, exercise_index.jsonl, and optionally answer.md. M4: exercise serialization. The parser reads each exercise section page by page and emits one JSON record per problem. record contains question, answer when an answer is printed immediately after the question, and number. The final problem fragment on page is carried into the next page before serialization so that page break does not split question into two records. Problem numbers are preserved for the matching stage. M5: answer partitioning. The pipeline determines whether numbering is absoluteone number identifies unique problem in the whole bookor relative, with numbers restarting across chapters. For absolute numbering, the answer chapter is serialized using the same page-wise procedure as M4. For relative numbering, the multilevel heading paths saved by M3 are used to partition the answer chapter before serialization. 14 Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks 1 2 3 Expository stream proof supervision Exercise stream textbook evaluation Source textbook Parse pages Recover hierarchy Separate streams Figure 6: High-level construction flow. Problems are serialized, printed answers are aligned under the books numbering scheme when available, and every candidate passes standalone-completeness check. M6: matching and filtering. Absolute-number records are joined directly on problem number. Relativenumber records are matched within their recovered chapter, using the section content when necessary. Books without printed answers follow third, unmatched branch. All branches then pass through completeness check that removes questions whose statements depend on an unprovided theorem or on the conclusion of another exercise. The module produces report with the number of exercises and answer coverage for each chapter. A.4. Four-stage proposition pipeline Each pure-content chapter is first split at Markdown headings while preserving its preamble, and the resulting sections are processed concurrently. The four semantic stages are as follows. 1. Proposition extraction. For every section, the model emits structured proposition records with type, number, label, title, content_tex, and proof_tex fields. 2. Reference resolution. book-level proposition library is built from the extracted records. For each proposition with proof, the model identifies both explicit ref citations and semantic references to earlier results, storing the matches in resolved_references. 3. Proof-gap audit. Each proof is checked for unverified lemma assumptions, omitted coordinate or operator transformations, and unsupported jumps marked by phrases such as obviously or clearly. candidate gap stores gap_statement, missing_logic, sub_proposition, and low/medium/high difficulty label. 4. Self-contained refinement. Each candidate sub-proposition is rewritten as an independent mathematical statement by declaring symbols, injecting required definitions, and preserving the source language. The chapter-level structured output contains the extracted propositions, resolved references, and candidate gaps. separate Proof QA JSONL stream distinguishes original proposition records from candidate subpropositions with an is_potential_gap flag. This schema describes the pipeline output; dataset-level acceptance, deduplication, and split policies are subsequent steps. A.5. Model-Quality Evaluation and Model Selection Evaluation Dimensions. We evaluate model quality along six dimensions: Completeness measures the completeness of extracted information; Accuracy assesses factual correctness; LaTeX Formatting evaluates compliance with LaTeX formatting requirements; Self-Containment measures whether each extracted item is independently understandable; Atomicity assesses whether each item represents single, coherent unit C/P Ratio measures cost-effectiveness in terms of the cost of generating single QA pair, with higher score indicating lower cost per pair. Model Configurations. We compare four configurations: Flash Thinking refers to gemini-3-flash-preview-thinking Flash Lite refers to gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview Pro Thinking refers to gemini-3.1-pro-preview-thinking Combined denotes pipeline combining Flash Thinking for primary extraction and auditing with Flash Lite for reference-semantic parsing. Results and Analysis. Figure 3 shows that Pro Thinking achieves strong performance in Completeness, Accuracy, LaTeX Formatting, Self-Containment, and Atomicity, but performs less favorably in C/P Ratio, indicating higher cost per generated QA pair. Flash Lite offers more cost-effective alternative, although its lower scores in Completeness and Self-Containment suggest potential limitations in information coverage and the independent interpretability of extracted items. Flash Thinking provides consistently strong performance across the five quality-oriented dimensions, while maintaining reasonable cost per QA pair. Notably, the Combined pipeline preserves competitive extraction quality while improving cost-effectiveness through the use of Flash Lite for reference-semantic parsing. Overall, these results suggest that the Combined pipeline offers favorable balance between extraction quality and the cost of generating individual QA pairs. 16 Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks B. Every condition is evaluated on the same textbook-native exercises from held-out books in the corresponding subject. Normalized chapter stages. Textbooks contain different numbers of chapters, so raw chapter indices are not directly comparable across books. For an example from book b, let i(x) be its zero-based chapter index and Nb the number of chapters in the book. We define its normalized position as p(x) = i(x)/Nb and assign it to progress stage S10p(x), yielding ten stages S0, . . . , S9. Examples from different books are interleaved within each stage, preserving their approximate within-book progression without imposing an arbitrary order over books. Gap QA makes locally omitted proof obligation explicit; all remaining examples are treated as Proof QA. Exposure schedules. The four schedules differ only in presentation order: SHUFFLE globally shuffles all examples. FORWARDGAP traverses stages from S0 to S9 and presents Gap before Non-gap examples within each stage.
